mcqs.question: In an AVL tree, what triggers a rotation?
options: A rotation runs on a fixed schedule regardless of tree state
A node's balance factor (left subtree height minus right subtree height) reaches -2 or +2 after an insert or delete
The tree exceeds a fixed maximum node count
Any search operation, regardless of whether the tree is balanced
mcqs.explanation: AVL's defining invariant is that every node's balance factor must stay within -1, 0, or +1; the moment a mutation pushes any node's balance factor outside that range, a rotation is required to restore it before the tree is considered valid again. Rotations aren't scheduled independently of tree state, aren't triggered by node count thresholds, and searches (which don't modify the tree) never trigger rebalancing.

mcqs.question: After a right rotation, why must the node that ends up lower in the tree have its height recomputed before the node that ends up higher?
options: Order doesn't matter as long as both heights get updated eventually
The higher node's height calculation depends on the lower node's new, post-rotation height, so computing it first would use a stale value
Height only needs to be recomputed for the tree's root, not for individual rotated nodes
Rotations don't change either node's height, so no recomputation is needed
mcqs.explanation: The node ending up higher (the new subtree root) has the other node as a child post-rotation, so its own height formula directly depends on that child's updated height — computing the higher node's height first would silently use the child's old, incorrect value. Order genuinely matters here, both nodes' heights typically change after a rotation (not just the root's), and skipping this recomputation entirely would leave balance factors wrong throughout the tree.

mcqs.question: What does the red-black invariant "no red node has a red child" combined with "equal black-height on every path" guarantee about the tree's height?
options: The tree's height is bounded by roughly 2 log n in the worst case — looser than AVL's bound, but still logarithmic
The tree is always perfectly balanced, identical to AVL
These invariants guarantee nothing about height, only about node coloring
The tree's height can still degrade to O(n) in rare cases
mcqs.explanation: Together, these coloring rules limit how much longer a path with alternating colors can be compared to an all-black path, which mathematically bounds worst-case height at roughly 2 log n — genuinely looser than AVL's tighter ~1.44 log n bound, but still logarithmic, not linear. Red-black trees are not identical to AVL trees in strictness, the invariants directly imply a real height bound (not merely a coloring rule with no consequence), and height cannot degrade to O(n) as long as the invariants hold.

mcqs.question: A system does vastly more lookups than insertions or deletions. Which self-balancing tree is the better fit, and why?
options: Red-black, because it always outperforms AVL on every metric
Neither — self-balancing trees provide no benefit for read-heavy workloads
AVL, because its stricter balance factor produces shorter trees on average, directly benefiting the dominant lookup workload at the cost of more rebalancing during the rarer mutations
AVL, because it requires no rotations at all during insertion
mcqs.explanation: AVL's tighter height bound (~1.44 log n versus red-black's ~2 log n) means shorter average paths, which directly speeds up the operation that dominates this workload — lookups — while its more frequent rebalancing during mutations matters less since those are rare here. Red-black doesn't universally outperform AVL, self-balancing trees do provide a real logarithmic-height benefit versus an unbalanced BST, and AVL still requires rotations during insertion, just typically balanced against faster lookups.

mcqs.question: You're told a library's ordered map is implemented with a "balanced tree," and you assume its height follows AVL's tight ~1.44 log n bound. What's the risk?
options: There's no risk — all balanced trees share the identical height bound

"Balanced" describes a family of guarantees, not one fixed bound — most production libraries actually use red-black trees, whose looser ~2 log n bound would make an AVL-based height estimate too optimistic
The risk only applies to trees with fewer than 100 nodes
This assumption is always safe since AVL is the standard implementation for ordered maps
mcqs.explanation: Different self-balancing schemes provide genuinely different height bounds despite all being called 'balanced,' and most general-purpose ordered-map implementations (TreeMap, std::map) use red-black trees, not AVL — so assuming the tighter AVL bound would underestimate actual tree height and any performance reasoning based on it. This isn't limited to small trees, and AVL is actually the less common choice in production ordered-map implementations, not the standard one.
